expectedText:
HEALTH CARE WORKER MINIMUM WAGE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's health care worker minimum wage, Labor Code § 1182.14 (added by Stats. 2023, Ch. 890 (SB 525), and amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 40, Sec. 27 (SB 159), effective June 29, 2024), as it may relate to Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc. It explains how the statute defines a “covered health care employee” and a “covered health care facility,” the tiered minimum wage schedules the statute sets for different categories of covered health care facility employers, the annual cost-of-living adjustment mechanism, the related salary-basis exemption threshold, the statute's enforcement mechanisms, its waiver program for certain clinics, and its preemption of local minimum wage ordinances for covered health care facility employees. This document does not itself determine whether Acme, Inc. or Jordan Lee's position meets the statute's coverage definitions, and it is not a substitute for consulting the full text of Labor Code § 1182.14 or a licensed attorney.

WHO IS A “COVERED HEALTH CARE EMPLOYEE”
California's health care worker minimum wage law defines a “covered health care employee” broadly to include an employee of a health care facility employer who provides patient care, health care services, or services supporting the provision of health care — a category the statute says includes, without limitation, nurses, physicians, caregivers, medical residents, patient care technicians, janitors, housekeeping staff, groundskeepers, guards, clerical and administrative workers, food service and gift shop workers, technical and ancillary services workers, medical coding and billing personnel, schedulers, call center and warehouse workers, and laundry workers, regardless of formal job title. The definition also extends to certain contracted or subcontracted employees, if the employee's employer contracts with the covered health care facility employer (or a contractor/subcontractor to it) to provide health care services or supporting services, and either the covered facility employer exercises the control over the employee's wages, hours, or working conditions associated with joint-employer status under the IWC wage orders, or the employee performs the contracted work primarily (more than half the employee's work time in a workweek) on the premises of a covered health care facility. The statute separately excludes certain categories from “covered health care employee” status, including employment as an outside salesperson, as well as (subject to conditions the statute itself states) certain public employees, delivery or waste-collection workers, and medical transportation workers who are not employed by the facility itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An employee of a health care facility employer who provides patient care, health care services, or services supporting the provision of health care, which includes, but is not limited to, employees performing work in the occupation of a nurse, physician, caregiver, medical resident, intern or fellow, patient care technician, janitor, housekeeping staff person, groundskeeper, guard, clerical worker, nonmanagerial administrative worker, food service worker, gift shop worker, technical and ancillary services worker, medical coding and medical billing personnel,
				  scheduler, call center and warehouse worker, and laundry worker, regardless of formal job title."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(b)(2)(A)(i), California Labor Code, definition of “covered health care employee” — core occupational list (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "“Covered health care employee” includes a contracted or subcontracted employee, if clauses (i) and (ii) apply:(i) The employee’s employer contracts with the covered health care facility employer, or with a contractor or subcontractor to the covered health care facility employer, to provide health care services, or services supporting the provision of health care."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(b)(2)(B)(i), California Labor Code, extension to certain contracted/subcontracted employees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "Notwithstanding subparagraph (A), “covered health care employee” does not include:(i) Employment as an outside salesperson."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(b)(2)(C)(i), California Labor Code, outside-salesperson exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: The occupation list quoted below is illustrative (“includes, but is not limited to”), not exhaustive, so whether a specific job title falls within or outside the definition can turn on the duties actually performed rather than the title used. The three citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(b)(2)) rather than independently authored sources — not independent of one another. This clause does not restate every exclusion the statute lists (e.g., the specific conditions for excluding certain public employees, delivery/waste-collection workers, or medical transportation workers), only the outside-salesperson exclusion is quoted in full below.

WHICH EMPLOYERS ARE A “COVERED HEALTH CARE FACILITY”
The statute defines “covered health care facility” through a long, specific list of licensed and certified facility types — including, among others, a facility within an integrated health care delivery system, a licensed general acute care hospital, a licensed acute psychiatric hospital, a special hospital, certain skilled nursing facilities, licensed home health agencies, clinics and dialysis clinics, psychology clinics, certain residential care facilities for the elderly, psychiatric health facilities, mental health rehabilitation centers, community and rural health clinics, urgent care clinics, certain ambulatory surgical centers, physician groups, and certain county correctional and mental health facilities. The statute then excludes two categories from that definition: a listed facility type that is owned, controlled, or operated by the state or a state agency of the executive branch (a carve-out that does not extend to a health care district or the University of California, which remain covered), and a tribal clinic exempt from licensure or an outpatient setting operated by a federally recognized tribe, tribal organization, or urban Indian organization.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Covered health care facility” means any of the following:(i) A facility or other work site that is part of an integrated health care delivery system.(ii) A licensed general acute care hospital, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 1250 of the Health and Safety Code, including a distinct part of any such hospital."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(b)(3)(A), California Labor Code, opening of the “covered health care facility” list (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "“Covered health care facility” does not include either of the following:(i) Any health care facility described in subparagraph (A) that is owned, controlled, or operated by the state or any state agency of the executive branch. As used in this subparagraph, “state agency” includes every state office, officer, department, division, bureau, board, and commission under the executive branch, including any constitutional offices or officers, California State University, or California Community College, but does not include a health care district or the University of California."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(b)(3)(B)(i), California Labor Code, state-agency-owned-facility exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This clause paraphrases and partially quotes a facility list running to roughly twenty separate subclauses in the statute (§ 1182.14(b)(3)(A)(i)-(xx)); it does not reproduce every listed facility type verbatim, so a facility not mentioned above may still be covered (or a facility resembling one on this list may still fall outside it) depending on its specific licensure and ownership structure. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(b)(3)) and are not independent of one another.

MINIMUM WAGE SCHEDULE — LARGE SYSTEMS, DIALYSIS CLINICS, AND HIGH-MEDICARE/MEDI-CAL-MIX HOSPITALS
For a covered health care facility employer with 10,000 or more full-time-equivalent employees (including as part of an integrated health care delivery system or health care system with that many), any employer that is or operates a dialysis clinic, or a covered facility owned or operated by a county with a population over 5,000,000 as of January 1, 2023, the statute sets a minimum wage of $23.00 per hour from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2025, $24.00 per hour from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026, and $25.00 per hour from July 1, 2026 onward (subject to the annual cost-of-living adjustment described elsewhere in this document). A separate, slower schedule applies to a hospital with a high governmental payor mix, an independent hospital with an elevated governmental payor mix, a rural independent covered health care facility, or a facility owned or operated by a county with a population under 250,000 as of January 1, 2023: $18.00 per hour from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2033, with 3.5 percent annual increases, then $25.00 per hour from July 1, 2033 onward. A county-owned, -affiliated, or -operated covered facility is not required to comply with any of these schedules before January 1, 2025.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "the minimum wage for all covered health care employees shall
				  be as follows:(A) From July 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025, inclusive, twenty-three dollars ($23) per hour.(B) From July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026, inclusive, twenty-four dollars ($24) per hour.(C) From July 1, 2026, and until adjusted pursuant to subdivision (d), twenty-five dollars ($25) per hour."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(c)(1), California Labor Code, minimum wage schedule for large systems/dialysis clinics/large counties (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "For any hospital that is a hospital with a high governmental payor mix, an independent hospital with an elevated governmental payor mix, a rural independent covered health care facility, or a covered health care facility that is owned, affiliated, or operated by a county with a population of less than 250,000 as of January 1, 2023, the minimum wage for all covered health care employees shall be as follows:(A) From July 1, 2024, to June 30, 2033, inclusive, eighteen dollars ($18) per hour, with 3.5 percent increases annually.(B) From July 1, 2033, and until adjusted pursuant to subdivision (d), twenty-five ($25) per hour."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(c)(2), California Labor Code, minimum wage schedule for high-governmental-payor-mix and rural hospitals (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of this subdivision, a covered health care facility that is county owned, affiliated, or operated shall not be required to comply with this subdivision before January 1, 2025. Commencing
				  January 1, 2025, a covered health care facility that is county owned, affiliated, or operated shall comply with the appropriate schedule described in this subdivision."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(c)(5), California Labor Code, delayed compliance date for county-owned facilities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This clause covers only two of the statute's four minimum-wage tiers; the tiers for specified clinics and for “all other” covered health care facility employers are addressed in a separate clause. The statutory terms “hospital with a high governmental payor mix,” “independent hospital with an elevated governmental payor mix,” and “rural independent covered health care facility” each carry their own detailed statutory definitions (turning on Medicare/Medi-Cal payor-mix percentages and facility classification data published by the Department of Health Care Access and Information) that this clause does not reproduce. The three citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(c)) and are not independent of one another.

MINIMUM WAGE SCHEDULE — SPECIFIED CLINICS AND ALL OTHER COVERED FACILITIES
For four specified categories of clinic — a community-clinic-type facility not operated by or affiliated with a licensed clinic, a licensed community clinic (and any associated intermittent clinic exempt from licensure), a rural health clinic that is not license-exempt, and an urgent care clinic owned by or affiliated with one of those clinics — the statute sets a minimum wage of $21.00 per hour from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2026, $22.00 per hour from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027, and $25.00 per hour from July 1, 2027 onward. For all other covered health care facility employers not otherwise addressed by one of the statute's schedules, the minimum wage is $21.00 per hour from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2026, $23.00 per hour from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2028, and $25.00 per hour from July 1, 2028 onward. Both schedules are subject to the annual cost-of-living adjustment described elsewhere in this document once each reaches its final $25.00-per-hour step.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For any health care facility specified in clauses (i) to (iv), inclusive, the minimum wage for all covered health care employees shall be as set forth in subparagraph (B).(i) A clinic as defined in subdivision (h) of Section 1206 of the Health and Safety Code, that is not operated by or affiliated with a clinic described in subdivision (b) of Section 1206 of the Health and Safety Code.(ii) A community clinic licensed under subdivision (a) of
				  Section 1204 of the Health and Safety Code, and any associated intermittent clinic exempt from licensure under subdivision (h) of Section 1206 of the Health and Safety Code.(iii) A rural health clinic, as defined in paragraph (1) of subdivision (l) of Section 1396d of Title 42 of the United States Code, that is not license-exempt.(iv) An urgent care clinic that is owned by or affiliated with a facility defined in clause (ii) or (iii)."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(c)(3), California Labor Code, minimum wage schedule for specified clinics (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "For all other covered health care facility employers, the minimum wage for all covered health care employees shall be as follows:(A) From July 1, 2024, to June 30, 2026, inclusive, twenty-one dollars ($21) per hour.(B) From July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2028, inclusive, twenty-three dollars ($23) per hour.(C) From July 1, 2028, and until adjusted pursuant to subdivision (d), twenty-five dollars ($25) per hour."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(c)(4), California Labor Code, minimum wage schedule for all other covered health care facility employers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: The four clinic categories in the first schedule are cross-defined by reference to specific subdivisions of Health and Safety Code §§ 1204 and 1206 and to 42 U.S.C. § 1396d(l)(1); this clause does not reproduce those cross-referenced definitions. The clinic categories described in the first schedule are also the categories eligible for the statute's separate 12-month waiver program, addressed in a separate clause. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(c)) and are not independent of one another.

ANNUAL COST-OF-LIVING ADJUSTMENT AFTER EACH SCHEDULE'S FINAL STEP
Once a covered health care facility employer's applicable minimum wage schedule reaches its final step (the point at which the statute's text says the wage is set at $25.00 per hour “until adjusted”), the California Director of Finance calculates an adjusted health care worker minimum wage on or before August 1 of the following year, and each August 1 after that. The adjustment increases the health care worker minimum wage by the lesser of 3.5 percent or the percentage change in the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' nonseasonally adjusted Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (U.S. CPI-W), comparing the most recent July 1-to-June 30 period to the preceding one, rounded to the nearest ten cents. Each calculated increase takes effect the following January 1. If the relevant CPI-W rate of change is negative, the statute provides that there is no increase or decrease to the health care worker minimum wage for that cycle.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "the Director of Finance shall calculate an adjusted minimum wage. The calculation shall increase the health care worker minimum wage by the lesser of 3.5 percent or the rate of change in the averages of the most recent July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period over the preceding July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period for the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics nonseasonally adjusted United States
				  Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (U.S. CPI-W). The result shall be rounded to the nearest ten cents ($0.10). Each adjusted health care worker minimum wage increase calculated under this subdivision shall take effect on the following January 1."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(d)(1), California Labor Code, the annual CPI-based adjustment calculation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "If the rate of change in the averages of the most recent July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period over the preceding July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period for the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics nonseasonally adjusted U.S. CPI-W is negative, there shall be no increase or decrease in the health care worker minimum wage pursuant to this subdivision on the following January 1."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(d)(2), California Labor Code, no decrease if CPI-W change is negative (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This mechanism only begins to operate after a given employer's tier reaches its statutory final step (2026, 2027, 2028, or 2033 depending on the tier); it does not itself set the initial step-up amounts described in the wage-schedule clauses. The statute does not describe what happens if the Director of Finance fails to publish a timely calculation. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(d)) and are not independent of one another.

SALARY-BASIS THRESHOLD TO QUALIFY AS EXEMPT FROM MINIMUM WAGE AND OVERTIME
For covered health care employment compensated on a salary basis, the statute requires the employee's monthly salary to equal no less than 150 percent of the applicable health care worker minimum wage, or 200 percent of the general California minimum wage under Labor Code § 1182.12, whichever amount is greater, for full-time employment, in order for the employee to qualify as exempt from the payment of minimum wage and overtime under California law. This threshold applies even where the employer is a political subdivision of the state, a health care district, the University of California, or a municipality.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For covered health care employment where the compensation of the employee is on a salary basis, the employee shall earn a monthly salary equivalent to no less than 150 percent of the health care worker minimum wage or 200 percent of the minimum wage, as described in Section 1182.12, whichever is greater, for full-time employment in order to qualify as exempt from the payment of minimum wage and overtime under the law of this state"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(g), California Labor Code, the health-care-specific exempt salary threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This clause states only the salary-level component of the exempt-status test; California's separate duties tests for exemption (e.g., executive, administrative, or professional duties) are not addressed by this statute or this clause, and satisfying this salary threshold alone does not establish that a given position is properly classified as exempt.

ENFORCEMENT, POSTING, AND EMPLOYEE NOTICE REQUIREMENTS
The statute makes the health care worker minimum wage enforceable by the Labor Commissioner through the same procedures used for other state minimum wage violations — Labor Code §§ 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1 — or by a covered worker through a civil action, with the same means and relief available for a violation of any other state minimum wage requirement. The statute separately requires the Department of Industrial Relations to amend, supplement, and republish the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders to be consistent with this section, and requires an employer subject to the statute to post a copy of the order as amended in a conspicuous location frequented by employees during the workday, and to provide each employee, on the effective date of the earliest minimum wage increase under the applicable tier, a written notice, in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information, stating which paragraph of the wage-schedule subdivision applies to the employer and the resulting health care worker minimum wage schedule applicable to the employee. The statute also states that the health care worker minimum wage constitutes the state minimum wage for covered health care employment for all purposes under the Labor Code and the wage orders.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A health care worker minimum wage shall be enforceable by the Labor Commissioner through the procedures set forth in Section 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1, or by a covered worker through a civil action, through the same means and with the same relief available for violation of any other state minimum wage requirement."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(f)(1), California Labor Code, Labor Commissioner and civil-action enforcement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "Post a copy of the order as amended, supplemented and republished by the Department of Industrial Relations under this section and keep it posted in a conspicuous location frequented by employees during the hours of the workday, as required by Section 1183."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(f)(2)(B)(i), California Labor Code, posting requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "Provide to each employee on the effective date of the earliest minimum wage increase pursuant to subdivision (c), a written notice, in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information to the employee, indicating the paragraph of subdivision (c) that applies to the employer and the health care worker minimum wage schedule applicable to the employee."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(f)(2)(B)(ii), California Labor Code, written employee notice requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This clause describes the enforcement pathways and the posting/notice obligations the statute lists; it does not itself constitute the posted wage order or the written notice the statute requires, and it does not describe the separate procedural requirements of each cross-referenced Labor Commissioner section (§§ 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, 1197.1) in detail. The posting/notice citation and the enforcement-mechanism citation below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(f)) and are not independent of one another.

THE DELAYED-COMPLIANCE WAIVER PROGRAM FOR SPECIFIED CLINICS
For the four specified clinic categories subject to the clinic minimum wage schedule described elsewhere in this document, the statute directs the Department of Industrial Relations, in collaboration with the Department of Health Care Access and Information, to administer a waiver program allowing a qualifying clinic to apply for a 12-month delay in that schedule, on a showing of specified financial hardship criteria (including audited financial statements, forecasting from an independent CPA, and balance sheets showing limited cash on hand and a low current ratio). If a waiver is issued, the wage-schedule step dates applicable to that clinic are postponed by 12 months. A clinic may apply for and receive a waiver in consecutive years, but the statute caps this relief: no waiver is available after July 1, 2032, and every eligible clinic must pay the fully adjusted wage beginning July 1, 2033, regardless of how many waivers it previously received.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The Department of Industrial Relations shall, in collaboration with the Department of Health Care Access and Information, administer a waiver program for covered health care facilities described in clauses (i) to (iv), inclusive, of subparagraph (A) of paragraph (3) of subdivision (c), which will allow a covered health care facility to apply for a 12-month delay in schedule of the health care minimum wage requirements in this section."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(i)(1), California Labor Code, the waiver program's existence and eligible clinics (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "If a covered health care facility is issued a waiver, all dates in clauses (i) to (iii), inclusive, of subparagraph (B) of paragraph (3) of subdivision (c), or any superseding dates pursuant to a previously issued waiver that are on or after the effective date of the issued waiver, are postponed by 12 months for that covered health care facility."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(i)(3), California Labor Code, the 12-month postponement effect of an issued waiver (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "a waiver shall not be available after July 1, 2032, and every covered health care facility described in clauses (i) to (iv), inclusive, of subparagraph (A) of paragraph (3) of subdivision (c) shall pay the adjusted wage required by subdivision (d) beginning July 1, 2033, regardless of whether the facility received any waivers."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(i)(6), California Labor Code, the July 1, 2032 cap on the waiver program (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This clause summarizes the waiver program's eligibility, effect, and outer time limit; it does not restate the full financial-hardship documentation the statute requires an applicant to submit, nor the separate notice-to-employees and posting obligations that apply once a waiver is issued. The three citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(i)) and are not independent of one another.

PREEMPTION OF LOCAL MINIMUM WAGE ORDINANCES FOR COVERED HEALTH CARE EMPLOYEES
The statute provides that a city, county, or city and county — including a charter city, charter county, or charter city and county — may not enact or enforce an ordinance, regulation, or administrative action that establishes, requires, imposes, limits, or otherwise relates to wages or compensation for covered health care facility employees, and that any such local measure enacted or taking effect after September 6, 2023 is void. This state occupation of the field does not, however, preclude any employer (including a public employer) from voluntarily establishing higher wage, salary, or compensation rates for its own employees or contracted/subcontracted employees, nor does it preclude a locality from adopting a minimum wage that applies uniformly across all industries rather than singling out covered health care facility employees. The statute also builds in future off-ramps from preemption: a locality may establish or enforce a health-care-specific minimum wage after January 1, 2034 (subject to ordinary preemption principles), and may enact an ordinance or take administrative action relating to compensation for covered health care facility employees after January 1, 2030 (also subject to ordinary preemption principles).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An ordinance, regulation, or administrative action applicable to a covered health care facility, as defined in this section, that establishes, requires, imposes, limits, or otherwise relates to wages or compensation for covered health care facility employees, as defined in this section, shall not be enacted or enforced in or by any city, county, city and county, including charter cities, charter counties, and charter cities and counties."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(j)(1)-(2), California Labor Code, the core preemption rule and voiding of post-September 6, 2023 local measures (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "This subdivision does not preclude any employer, including a city, county, city and county, including charter cities, charter counties, and charter cities and counties, that employs health care employees, from establishing higher wage, salary, or compensation rates for its employees or contracted or subcontracted employees."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(j)(3), California Labor Code, exception allowing voluntarily higher employer-set wages (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  "This subdivision does not preclude a city, county, city and county, including charter cities, charter counties, and charter cities and counties, from establishing or enforcing a minimum wage applicable to covered health care facility employees, as defined in this section, after January 1, 2034. Any such ordinance, regulation, or administrative action shall be evaluated under ordinary preemption principles."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(j)(5), California Labor Code, the January 1, 2034 sunset on health-care-specific preemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1182.14&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This clause describes the preemption rule and its stated exceptions as of the statutory text fetched; it does not evaluate whether any particular local ordinance, before or after the stated dates, would in fact be preempted, which the statute itself says is to be judged under “ordinary preemption principles” rather than a rule this clause can state in advance. This entire subdivision is itself conditional — the statute says it applies only if the provisions of the section requiring health care worker minimum wages take effect. The three citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(j)) and are not independent of one another.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF RECEIPT
Jordan Lee acknowledges having received this information sheet describing California's health care worker minimum wage, Labor Code § 1182.14.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Signature: _______________________________________________
Date: _______________

On behalf of Acme, Inc.:
Signature: _______________________________________________
Date: _______________

expectedJSON.body: The statute defines “covered health care facility” through a long, specific list of licensed and certified facility types — including, among others, a facility within an integrated health care delivery system, a licensed general acute care hospital, a licensed acute psychiatric hospital, a special hospital, certain skilled nursing facilities, licensed home health agencies, clinics and dialysis clinics, psychology clinics, certain residential care facilities for the elderly, psychiatric health facilities, mental health rehabilitation centers, community and rural health clinics, urgent care clinics, certain ambulatory surgical centers, physician groups, and certain county correctional and mental health facilities. The statute then excludes two categories from that definition: a listed facility type that is owned, controlled, or operated by the state or a state agency of the executive branch (a carve-out that does not extend to a health care district or the University of California, which remain covered), and a tribal clinic exempt from licensure or an outpatient setting operated by a federally recognized tribe, tribal organization, or urban Indian organization.

expectedJSON.body: Once a covered health care facility employer's applicable minimum wage schedule reaches its final step (the point at which the statute's text says the wage is set at $25.00 per hour “until adjusted”), the California Director of Finance calculates an adjusted health care worker minimum wage on or before August 1 of the following year, and each August 1 after that. The adjustment increases the health care worker minimum wage by the lesser of 3.5 percent or the percentage change in the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' nonseasonally adjusted Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (U.S. CPI-W), comparing the most recent July 1-to-June 30 period to the preceding one, rounded to the nearest ten cents. Each calculated increase takes effect the following January 1. If the relevant CPI-W rate of change is negative, the statute provides that there is no increase or decrease to the health care worker minimum wage for that cycle.

the Director of Finance shall calculate an adjusted minimum wage. The calculation shall increase the health care worker minimum wage by the lesser of 3.5 percent or the rate of change in the averages of the most recent July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period over the preceding July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period for the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics nonseasonally adjusted United States
				  Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (U.S. CPI-W). The result shall be rounded to the nearest ten cents ($0.10). Each adjusted health care worker minimum wage increase calculated under this subdivision shall take effect on the following January 1.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, no decrease if CPI-W change is negative
citations.quote: If the rate of change in the averages of the most recent July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period over the preceding July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period for the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics nonseasonally adjusted U.S. CPI-W is negative, there shall be no increase or decrease in the health care worker minimum wage pursuant to this subdivision on the following January 1.

The statute does not describe what happens if the Director of Finance fails to publish a timely calculation. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(d)) and are not independent of one another.

expectedJSON.body: For covered health care employment compensated on a salary basis, the statute requires the employee's monthly salary to equal no less than 150 percent of the applicable health care worker minimum wage, or 200 percent of the general California minimum wage under Labor Code § 1182.12, whichever amount is greater, for full-time employment, in order for the employee to qualify as exempt from the payment of minimum wage and overtime under California law. This threshold applies even where the employer is a political subdivision of the state, a health care district, the University of California, or a municipality.

citations.quote: For covered health care employment where the compensation of the employee is on a salary basis, the employee shall earn a monthly salary equivalent to no less than 150 percent of the health care worker minimum wage or 200 percent of the minimum wage, as described in Section 1182.12, whichever is greater, for full-time employment in order to qualify as exempt from the payment of minimum wage and overtime under the law of this state

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states only the salary-level component of the exempt-status test; California's separate duties tests for exemption (e.g., executive, administrative, or professional duties) are not addressed by this statute or this clause, and satisfying this salary threshold alone does not establish that a given position is properly classified as exempt.

expectedJSON.body: The statute makes the health care worker minimum wage enforceable by the Labor Commissioner through the same procedures used for other state minimum wage violations — Labor Code §§ 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1 — or by a covered worker through a civil action, with the same means and relief available for a violation of any other state minimum wage requirement. The statute separately requires the Department of Industrial Relations to amend, supplement, and republish the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders to be consistent with this section, and requires an employer subject to the statute to post a copy of the order as amended in a conspicuous location frequented by employees during the workday, and to provide each employee, on the effective date of the earliest minimum wage increase under the applicable tier, a written notice, in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information, stating which paragraph of the wage-schedule subdivision applies to the employer and the resulting health care worker minimum wage schedule applicable to the employee. The statute also states that the health care worker minimum wage constitutes the state minimum wage for covered health care employment for all purposes under the Labor Code and the wage orders.

citations.quote: A health care worker minimum wage shall be enforceable by the Labor Commissioner through the procedures set forth in Section 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1, or by a covered worker through a civil action, through the same means and with the same relief available for violation of any other state minimum wage requirement.

citations.quote: Post a copy of the order as amended, supplemented and republished by the Department of Industrial Relations under this section and keep it posted in a conspicuous location frequented by employees during the hours of the workday, as required by Section 1183.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, written employee notice requirement
citations.quote: Provide to each employee on the effective date of the earliest minimum wage increase pursuant to subdivision (c), a written notice, in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information to the employee, indicating the paragraph of subdivision (c) that applies to the employer and the health care worker minimum wage schedule applicable to the employee.

expectedJSON.body: For the four specified clinic categories subject to the clinic minimum wage schedule described elsewhere in this document, the statute directs the Department of Industrial Relations, in collaboration with the Department of Health Care Access and Information, to administer a waiver program allowing a qualifying clinic to apply for a 12-month delay in that schedule, on a showing of specified financial hardship criteria (including audited financial statements, forecasting from an independent CPA, and balance sheets showing limited cash on hand and a low current ratio). If a waiver is issued, the wage-schedule step dates applicable to that clinic are postponed by 12 months. A clinic may apply for and receive a waiver in consecutive years, but the statute caps this relief: no waiver is available after July 1, 2032, and every eligible clinic must pay the fully adjusted wage beginning July 1, 2033, regardless of how many waivers it previously received.

expectedJSON.body: The statute provides that a city, county, or city and county — including a charter city, charter county, or charter city and county — may not enact or enforce an ordinance, regulation, or administrative action that establishes, requires, imposes, limits, or otherwise relates to wages or compensation for covered health care facility employees, and that any such local measure enacted or taking effect after September 6, 2023 is void. This state occupation of the field does not, however, preclude any employer (including a public employer) from voluntarily establishing higher wage, salary, or compensation rates for its own employees or contracted/subcontracted employees, nor does it preclude a locality from adopting a minimum wage that applies uniformly across all industries rather than singling out covered health care facility employees. The statute also builds in future off-ramps from preemption: a locality may establish or enforce a health-care-specific minimum wage after January 1, 2034 (subject to ordinary preemption principles), and may enact an ordinance or take administrative action relating to compensation for covered health care facility employees after January 1, 2030 (also subject to ordinary preemption principles).

citations.cite: California Labor Code, the core preemption rule and voiding of post-September 6, 2023 local measures
citations.quote: An ordinance, regulation, or administrative action applicable to a covered health care facility, as defined in this section, that establishes, requires, imposes, limits, or otherwise relates to wages or compensation for covered health care facility employees, as defined in this section, shall not be enacted or enforced in or by any city, county, city and county, including charter cities, charter counties, and charter cities and counties.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, exception allowing voluntarily higher employer-set wages
citations.quote: This subdivision does not preclude any employer, including a city, county, city and county, including charter cities, charter counties, and charter cities and counties, that employs health care employees, from establishing higher wage, salary, or compensation rates for its employees or contracted or subcontracted employees.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, the January 1, 2034 sunset on health-care-specific preemption
citations.quote: This subdivision does not preclude a city, county, city and county, including charter cities, charter counties, and charter cities and counties, from establishing or enforcing a minimum wage applicable to covered health care facility employees, as defined in this section, after January 1, 2034. Any such ordinance, regulation, or administrative action shall be evaluated under ordinary preemption principles.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause describes the preemption rule and its stated exceptions as of the statutory text fetched; it does not evaluate whether any particular local ordinance, before or after the stated dates, would in fact be preempted, which the statute itself says is to be judged under “ordinary preemption principles” rather than a rule this clause can state in advance. This entire subdivision is itself conditional — the statute says it applies only if the provisions of the section requiring health care worker minimum wages take effect. The three citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(j)) and are not independent of one another.
